It reported intrusion efforts against 128 organisations in 42 countries outside Ukraine, and that "the Russian targeting we've identified has been successful 29 percent of the time". It credited Ukraine's rapid move of government data into the public cloud, hosted in data centres across Europe (Russia had hit a government data centre with a cruise missile), and endpoint protection that could be updated quickly.

**Carnegie, December 2022.** In a paper for the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, analyst Jon Bateman concluded that "Russia's cyber operations in Ukraine have apparently not had much military impact", that intelligence collection, not fires, was likely their main focus, and that "perhaps the most important" constraints were "inadequate Russian cyber capacity, weaknesses in Russia's non-cyber institutions, and exceptional defensive efforts by Ukraine and its partners". It also notes that "Most Western observers agree" on the limited strategic impact, "but there is less consensus on why", and calls its findings "tentative insights" representing "one reasonable interpretation of fragmentary, conflicting, and evolving data".

**Mandiant, November 2023.** Russia's 2022 grid attack shows an OT capability that, Mandiant warned, could be developed "against other SCADA systems" too, and it might have been developed in as little as two months. Limited impact so far is not limited capability.

blocks.title: Claims about the cyber war, and how well each is supported

scenes.caption: Four common claims about cyber in the war. The tone shows support in the sources read here: green well documented, grey contested or unknown.
Destructive operations against Ukraine were frequent: documented by Microsoft, ESET, Mandiant and governments, with named malware and dates.
Spillover beyond Ukraine: the Viasat attack cut users across Europe, documented by Viasat and the NCSC. Microsoft also reports espionage outside Ukraine.
Cyber had little military impact: the majority view, per Carnegie, yet built on what its author calls fragmentary, conflicting and evolving data. Hold it as a tentative finding.

Cyber timed with strikes: Microsoft reported Russia coupling some cyberattacks with conventional weapons; for the October 2022 grid attack Mandiant saw an overlap but lacked evidence of a link. Keep it open.

blocks.md:
**Spillover and norms.** The Viasat attack reached far beyond its believed military target: personal and commercial users and wind farms in central Europe lost connectivity. That is the kind of effect norm (f) and international humanitarian law worry about, and part of why the UK and the EU named Russia for it on the same day. The NCF's 2023 document adds another worry from the same war: cyber criminals and hacktivists "explicitly aligning themselves with each side's political objectives", showing "the potential growth of ideologically driven cyber-attacks outside of any state influence or control at all".

**Practices the sources credit**, which transfer to any organisation:

- Keep critical data and services out of a single physical location: cloud hosting and tested offline backups.
- Keep endpoint protection connected and updatable, so new wiper detections arrive in hours.
- Share fast across companies and national CERTs, as ESET and CERT-UA did with Industroyer2.
- For physical services, practise running without the network.

Both "cyber war turned out to be hype" and "cyber decided the war" overclaim. The public record is partial: most operations and most defensive successes are classified or unpublished. State which source a conclusion comes from, what data it rests on, and whether its author calls it a finding or a hypothesis.

blocks.question: What does Microsoft's figure 'successful 29 percent of the time' refer to?
options: The share of all Ukrainian organisations that were breached
The share of Russian targeting that Microsoft itself identified which succeeded, in Microsoft's own data
The share of Russian wipers that destroyed data
The share of NATO governments compromised during the war
blocks.explain: The sentence is about 'the Russian targeting we've identified'. It is a statistic over Microsoft's visibility, not over all of Ukraine, all wipers or all NATO governments. Always ask what population a percentage is computed over.

blocks.question: Which statement is best supported by the sources in this lesson?
options: Russia's cyber operations were coordinated with every missile strike
Cyber operations played no role at all in the war
Russian cyber operations in Ukraine were frequent and real, but their military impact appears limited, and the reasons are still debated
Ukraine's defence succeeded only because Russia chose not to attack
blocks.explain: Microsoft, ESET and Mandiant document many operations; Carnegie reports a majority view of limited military impact with 'less consensus on why'. Mandiant declined to link the October attack to missile strikes, and nobody claims cyber played no role.

lessons.title: North Korea's revenue operations: banks, crypto and IT workers

blocks.md:
Most states hack to learn or to break things. North Korea also hacks to get paid. Treasury says its Bluenoroff group was formed "to earn revenue illicitly in response to increased global sanctions", partly for "its growing nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs".

**Bangladesh Bank, February 2016.** After spearphishing into the bank's network, the operators reached the computers connected to **SWIFT** (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, the bank-to-bank payment messaging network) and, in DOJ's words, "sent fraudulently authenticated SWIFT messages directing the Federal Reserve Bank of NY to transfer funds". The theft netted USD 81 million. Treasury adds that the operators made over 36 large transfer requests, attempting USD 851 million in total, "before a typographical error alerted personnel to prevent the additional funds from being stolen". The 2018 complaint ties the same team to Sony Pictures and WannaCry (both in *A history of hacking*).

**From banks to crypto.** A February 2021 [indictment](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/three-north-korean-military-hackers-indicted-wide-ranging-scheme-commit-cyberattacks-and) charged three programmers of the RGB with a conspiracy to steal and extort more than USD 1.3 billion: attempted bank thefts of more than USD 1.2 billion from 2015 to 2019, ATM "cash-out" schemes the US calls FASTCash, fake cryptocurrency trading apps that installed a backdoor (the AppleJeus family), and thefts from cryptocurrency companies. On 26 February 2025 the [FBI](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA250226) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of about USD 1.5 billion in virtual assets from the exchange Bybit, activity it calls "TraderTraitor", and asked exchanges and other services to block the laundering addresses. How that theft worked is taught in *Smart contract and blockchain security*.

blocks.title: How the remote IT worker scheme works, and where it can be caught

scenes.caption: North Korean IT workers abroad apply for remote jobs at foreign companies using stolen or fake identities, sometimes with help from people in other countries.
The company ships a laptop to a US address. A paid facilitator hosts it in a 'laptop farm' and connects remote-control hardware, so the worker abroad appears to be in the US.
Salary flows to accounts of shell companies set up by facilitators, then onward. DOJ says such schemes fund the regime, including its weapons programmes.
Some workers also steal: export-controlled data from a defence contractor, and cryptocurrency from a blockchain firm in one indicted case.
Catch points: identity proofing at hiring, where the laptop really is, remote-control hardware on it, logins from hosting networks, and who receives the salary.

blocks.md: **Remote IT workers.** A [May 2022 State Department, Treasury and FBI advisory](https://ofac.treasury.gov/media/923126/download?inline) said such workers can individually earn "more than USD 300,000 a year in some cases", and teams "more than USD 3 million annually", much of it supporting regime priorities including weapons programmes. On 30 June 2025 [DOJ announced](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-coordinated-nationwide-actions-combat-north-korean-remote) searches of 29 suspected laptop farms in 16 states and seizures of 29 accounts, 21 websites and about 200 computers.

In one indicted scheme, from about 2021 to October 2024, the defendants used the identities of more than 80 US persons to get jobs at more than 100 US companies, hosted company laptops with **KVM** ("keyboard-video-mouse") switches for remote control, and ran shell companies to receive pay. One worker took data controlled under ITAR (International Traffic in Arms Regulations, US export rules for defence technology). In another case, four North Koreans were charged after two of them, hired by blockchain firms under false identities, stole cryptocurrency worth over USD 900,000, one by modifying smart contracts, and laundered it through the Tornado Cash mixer.

blocks.code:
# Verification signals for remote hires (SYNTHETIC records).
# No single signal proves fraud; several together mean "verify in person".
SIGNALS = {
    "ship_mismatch":  (2, "laptop shipped to an address that is not the hire's home"),
    "kvm_seen":       (3, "KVM or remote-control hardware on the laptop's USB bus"),
    "hosting_logins": (2, "logins from VPN or hosting networks, not home broadband"),
    "new_llc_payee":  (2, "salary paid to a recently formed company, not the person"),
    "id_reused":      (3, "identity details match another employee or applicant"),
}
hires = {
    "dev-0412": ["ship_mismatch"],
    "dev-0419": ["ship_mismatch", "kvm_seen", "hosting_logins", "new_llc_payee"],
    "ops-0177": ["hosting_logins"],
}
for who, seen in hires.items():
    score = sum(SIGNALS[s][0] for s in seen)
    action = "escalate: verify identity in person" if score >= 5 else "no action"
    print(f"{who}: score {score:2} -> {action}")
    for s in seen:
        print("    -", SIGNALS[s][1])

# Output:
# dev-0412: score  2 -> no action
#     - laptop shipped to an address that is not the hire's home
# dev-0419: score  9 -> escalate: verify identity in person
#     - laptop shipped to an address that is not the hire's home
#     - KVM or remote-control hardware on the laptop's USB bus
#     - logins from VPN or hosting networks, not home broadband
#     - salary paid to a recently formed company, not the person
# ops-0177: score  2 -> no action
#     - logins from VPN or hosting networks, not home broadband
blocks.caption: Verification signals for remote hires, scored on synthetic records. The signals come from the scheme DOJ describes: shipping addresses, KVM hardware, hosting-network logins, shell-company payees and reused identities.

blocks.md:
**Defender's view.** Prevent: verify identity at hiring with documents checked against a live person, ship equipment only to a verified home address, and pay only accounts in the employee's own name. Detect: device inventory that flags remote-control hardware, logins from VPN or hosting networks instead of home broadband, and one identity's details appearing on several applications. Respond: restrict access first, preserve evidence, involve legal counsel and report to law enforcement; paying a sanctioned entity can itself create legal exposure.

For crypto firms the controls are those of *Smart contract and blockchain security*: protect signing keys, check what is really being signed, and monitor for abnormal withdrawals, because stolen funds are converted fast.

Base checks on verification signals, never on nationality, accent or ethnicity. The schemes used stolen identities of real people, often US citizens, so profiling would both miss them and discriminate against genuine applicants. The question is always "is this person who they say they are, where they say they are?"

blocks.question: In the laptop-farm schemes DOJ describes, what job did the KVM switches do?
options: They let workers abroad control company laptops remotely, so the laptops appeared to be used from inside the US
They encrypted the stolen data before exfiltration
They mined cryptocurrency on the company's hardware
They hid the laptops from the company's asset inventory
blocks.explain: DOJ says facilitators hosted company laptops and connected them to KVM hardware 'designed to allow for remote access'. The laptop's location is real; the person at the keyboard is not where the company thinks. Nothing describes encryption, mining or hiding from inventory.

blocks.question: The Bangladesh Bank operators attempted to move USD 851 million but stole USD 81 million. According to Treasury, what stopped the rest?
options: SWIFT's software rejected messages over a fixed limit
The bank's antivirus detected the malware during the transfers
The Federal Reserve required two-factor approval for every transfer
A typographical error alerted personnel, who then prevented the additional transfers
blocks.explain: Treasury: the operators made over 36 large transfer requests 'before a typographical error alerted personnel'. The sources describe no automatic limit, antivirus detection or extra approval step stopping the transfers.

lessons.title: Threat-informed defence: from a state threat to your detections

blocks.md:
You now know what states want, how they organise, how governments name them and how they respond. The defender's question is narrower: *which of their behaviours could we see and stop tomorrow?* **Threat-informed defence** is the practice of answering that systematically; MITRE's [Center for Threat-Informed Defense](https://ctid.mitre.org/) (CTID) describes its work as building on MITRE ATT&CK, "an important foundation for threat-informed defense".

A workable loop for a state threat:

1. **Pick relevant groups** by sector and purpose: a water utility starts with actors assessed to pre-position in water; a crypto firm with North Korean revenue groups.
2. **Read the joint advisories** about them, from CISA, the NCSC and partners (such as AA24-038A and AA25-239A), and their ATT&CK group entries.
3. **Map behaviours to techniques**, noting the ATT&CK version used.
4. **Compare with tested detections and mitigations**; rank gaps by how many relevant groups use each technique.
5. **Hunt, fix and re-test**, then repeat when the next advisory appears.

**ATT&CK group entries.** Each group page summarises attribution and lists techniques with references. For example, [G1017 Volt Typhoon](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1017/) is "a People's Republic of China (PRC) state-sponsored actor that has been active since at least 2021"; [G0034 Sandworm Team](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0034/) "has been attributed to Russia's General Staff Main Intelligence Directorate (GRU) Main Center for Special Technologies (GTsST) military unit 74455"; [G0032 Lazarus Group](https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0032/) is "attributed to the Reconnaissance General Bureau (RGB)".

Two cautions. Names do not line up perfectly: AA25-239A warns that vendor names "may not be a 1:1 correlation to the authoring agencies' understanding". And technique IDs move between versions: as you saw in *Cyber threat intelligence*, a 2024 advisory's T1070.001 (Clear Windows Event Logs) is T1685.005 in today's ATT&CK.

blocks.title: A synthetic advisory against our detections: where the gaps are

scenes.caption: Rows: techniques from a synthetic joint advisory. Columns: whether group A or B is said to use each, and whether we have a tested detection (1 yes, 0 no).
Gaps are rows with 0 in the detection column. T1190, exploiting public-facing applications, is used by both groups and is undetected: the first priority.
T1070.001 looks undetected under its old id, but our rule is tagged T1685.005, the same technique today. After remapping it counts as covered.
Coverage is 3 of 6 techniques, but 5 of 9 group-technique uses. Weighting by relevance shows what matters to this organisation, not just to the list.

blocks.code:
# Coverage check: SYNTHETIC advisory for groups A and B, toy detections.
advisory = {   # technique (ATT&CK v14 id): groups said to use it
    "T1190":     ["A", "B"],   # Exploit Public-Facing Application
    "T1078":     ["A", "B"],   # Valid Accounts
    "T1003.003": ["A"],         # OS Credential Dumping: NTDS
    "T1070.001": ["A", "B"],   # Clear Windows Event Logs (old id)
    "T1484.001": ["B"],         # Group Policy Modification
    "T1090":     ["A"],         # Proxy
}
moved = {"T1070.001": "T1685.005"}       # id moves since v14
detections = {"T1078", "T1685.005", "T1003.003"}  # our tested rules (v20)

rows = []
for t, groups in advisory.items():
    now = moved.get(t, t)
    covered = now in detections
    rows.append((len(groups), t, now, covered))
rows.sort(key=lambda r: (r[3], -r[0]))   # gaps, then most used
for n, t, now, ok in rows:
    tag = "covered" if ok else "GAP"
    alias = f"(now {now})" if now != t else ""
    print(f"{tag:8} {t:10} {alias:16} used by {n} group(s)")
done = sum(r[3] for r in rows)
print(f"coverage: {done}/{len(rows)}; weighted by groups: "
      f"{sum(r[0] for r in rows if r[3])}/{sum(r[0] for r in rows)}")

# Output:
# GAP      T1190                       used by 2 group(s)
# GAP      T1484.001                   used by 1 group(s)
# GAP      T1090                       used by 1 group(s)
# covered  T1078                       used by 2 group(s)
# covered  T1070.001  (now T1685.005)  used by 2 group(s)
# covered  T1003.003                   used by 1 group(s)
# coverage: 3/6; weighted by groups: 5/9
blocks.caption: Coverage of a synthetic advisory against a toy detection set, after remapping moved technique ids. Gaps are sorted first, and by how many relevant groups use them.

blocks.md:
**Beyond detections.** Advisories also list mitigations, and many of the most valuable ones are not alerts: replace end-of-life edge devices, require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, segment IT from OT, keep offline backups of identity systems, and, for revenue threats, harden hiring and payment processes. Track these in the same coverage table as "mitigated" rather than "detected".

**Test, do not assume.** A rule tagged with a technique is not coverage until it has fired on a realistic test. Emulating a relevant group's published behaviours in your own environment, under an agreed plan, is how you find out; *Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming* teaches how.

A state threat becomes useful to a defender at the level of techniques and processes: which behaviours of which relevant groups can we prevent, detect or recover from, tested, today? Everything else in this course (purpose, attribution, law, responses) helps choose the groups and set priorities.

blocks.question: Your coverage table shows four gaps. Which should normally go first?
options: The technique used by every relevant group that you can neither detect nor mitigate
The technique with the highest ATT&CK id number
The technique most recently added to ATT&CK
Whichever technique is easiest to write a rule for, regardless of use
blocks.explain: Prioritise by relevance and exposure: a behaviour shared by all the groups you care about and currently invisible is the biggest risk. ID numbers and recency say nothing about risk; easy rules are fine to do too, but not first by default.

blocks.question: AA25-239A says vendor names 'may not be a 1:1 correlation' to the agencies' understanding. What does that mean for your coverage work?
options: Ignore vendor reports and use only government advisories
Keep techniques from each source labelled with that source, rather than merging every vendor report under one actor name
Assume every vendor name for the actor describes exactly the same operators
Stop mapping techniques until the names are reconciled
blocks.explain: Names cover overlapping but not identical activity. Labelling by source keeps you honest about what was seen by whom, while still using all the reports. Discarding vendor data, assuming equality, or stopping work are all worse.

lessons.title: Putting it together: a state-threat brief, and practice

blocks.md:
A headline lands on Monday: *"Foreign state hackers found in water systems."* Your manager asks two questions: is it true, and what do we do? Everything in this course turns into five questions you can answer in an hour:

1. **Purpose**: espionage, disruption, influence, pre-positioning or revenue? This predicts what is at risk.
2. **Claim**: who said it (government, vendor, journalist), at which level (technical, operational, strategic), in which exact words and with what confidence? Is anything contested?
3. **Context**: does it touch a norm or legal line that governments cite, and has there been a response (advisory, indictment, sanctions, disruption)?
4. **Relevance**: do we run the targeted technology or sector? Which ATT&CK techniques does the advisory map, and which do we cover?
5. **Action**: what do we hunt, fix and prepare this week, and who owns it?

blocks.title: From headline to actions in five questions

scenes.caption: A headline is a claim about someone else's claim. Start by finding the primary source it rests on.
From the source, answer purpose and claim: what was the operation for, who says so, at which level and how confidently.
Then relevance: compare the advisory's technologies and techniques with your own inventory and coverage.
End with owned actions: hunt, fix, prepare. The brief's value is measured by these, not by naming a country.

blocks.code:
# Check each attribution sentence in a draft brief: who said it, which
# rung of the ladder it is on, and how sure they were. (SYNTHETIC draft)
import re
draft = [
    "Russia hacked the satellite network.",
    "The UK NCSC assessed Russia was almost certainly responsible (May 2022).",
    "Vendor X links the wiper to cluster UNC-0000 with moderate confidence.",
    "The group is a front for a contractor.",
]
WORDS = r"almost certainly|highly likely|likely|realistic possibility|unlikely"
CONF = r"(high|moderate|low) confidence"
WHO = r"\b(NCSC|CISA|FBI|DOJ|vendor|Mandiant|Microsoft|ESET|government)\b"
for s in draft:
    missing = []
    if not re.search(WHO, s, re.I):
        missing.append("who says so")
    if not (re.search(WORDS, s, re.I) or re.search(CONF, s, re.I)):
        missing.append("likelihood or confidence")
    print(("OK    " if not missing else "FIX   ") + s)
    if missing:
        print("      missing:", ", ".join(missing))

# Output:
# FIX   Russia hacked the satellite network.
#       missing: who says so, likelihood or confidence
# OK    The UK NCSC assessed Russia was almost certainly responsible (May 2022).
# OK    Vendor X links the wiper to cluster UNC-0000 with moderate confidence.
# FIX   The group is a front for a contractor.
#       missing: who says so, likelihood or confidence
blocks.caption: A draft-checking aid: every attribution sentence should say who makes the claim and how likely or how confident they are. Real review is done by people; this catches the habit.

blocks.md:
**A one-paragraph brief that passes the checks** (synthetic organisation, real sources):

*Bottom line: replace our two end-of-life branch routers this month and hunt for admin-tool use on domain controllers. Basis: in February 2024 US agencies assessed "with high confidence" that PRC state-sponsored actors known as Volt Typhoon were pre-positioning in water and other sectors to disrupt them in a crisis (AA24-038A); a December 2023 court-authorised operation removed their malware from hundreds of US routers, most of them end-of-life (DOJ). China's CVERC disputes the attribution; the vendors it cited reject its claims. We run the same router class; we have detections for 3 of the 6 techniques in our test set. Owner: infrastructure lead, review in 30 days.*

Every claim carries its source, its words and its date; the contested claim is reported, not hidden; the actions are owned.

**Practise legally.** Work only with public material, your own lab, or platforms that invite you.

- [MITRE ATT&CK CTI training](https://attack.mitre.org/resources/learn-more-about-attack/training/cti/): free modules on mapping reports to ATT&CK and comparing groups.
- [CCDCOE Cyber Law Toolkit](https://cyberlaw.ccdcoe.org/wiki/Main_Page): hypothetical scenarios inspired by real incidents, each with a full legal analysis; try your own answer before reading theirs.
- Read [AA24-038A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-038a) and [AA25-239A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa25-239a) end to end, and write the five-question brief for an imaginary utility and an imaginary telecom provider.
- [CyberDefenders](https://cyberdefenders.org/blueteam-ctf-challenges/) and [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/): defensive investigations, including threat intelligence and timeline challenges.

State cyber operations are strategy carried out through ordinary intrusion steps. Read the purpose, keep every attribution claim tied to its source and exact words, know which legal and diplomatic lines are being argued about, and turn it all into tested defences against the behaviours of the groups that matter to you.

blocks.question: A vendor blog says 'Country X is behind the attack'; no government has commented. How should your brief state it?
options: Country X attacked the company
Governments have confirmed Country X is responsible
It is impossible to say anything until a court rules
Vendor V attributes the activity to a group it links to Country X, with the confidence V states; no government attribution so far
blocks.explain: Name who made the claim, at what level and with what confidence, and say what is missing. The first two options strip or invent the source; waiting for a court would mean saying nothing useful for years.

blocks.question: Which part of a state-threat brief is most directly measured by whether the brief was worth writing?
options: The name of the country responsible
The number of sources cited
The owned actions: what will be hunted, fixed or prepared, by whom and by when
The length of the background section
blocks.explain: As the prerequisite course stressed, intelligence is judged by the decisions it enables. A country name or a long source list may be accurate and still change nothing.
